items.title: Trump waives several Russia sanctions as row with Zelensky intensifies
items.summary: Donald Trump has blocked several congressionally mandated sanctions against Russia by executive order, intensifying an ongoing diplomatic rift with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. The waived measures include potential tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy.

also.title: Trump exempts Russia from further sanctions mandated by new law
also.note: Financial Times highlights the statutory aspect of the decision by focusing on the exemption of measures mandated by new legislation rather than the personal dispute with Zelensky.

also.title: Trump waives Russia sanctions as rift with Zelenskyy widens
also.note: Al Jazeera frames the story identically to the BBC by pairing the waiver directly with the widening rift between Trump and Zelenskyy.

also.author: David Zimmermann
also.title: Trump waives Russia sanctions ordered by law named for Lindsey Graham
also.note: Washington Examiner focuses on the domestic political origin of the sanctions by noting the legislation was named for Senator Lindsey Graham.

brief.what: US President Donald Trump issued an executive order blocking several sanctions against Russia shortly before their implementation, including powers to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas. The move suspends measures enacted by Congress targeting Russian financial institutions, senior officials, and Moscow's shadow fleet.
brief.who: US President Donald Trump waived the measures, facing harsh criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US congressional Democrats, while Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev welcomed the executive order.
brief.context: Bilateral relations between Washington and Kyiv have rapidly deteriorated after the US arranged to import Russian diesel to alleviate domestic fuel prices. Friction escalated further following mutual strikes on energy infrastructure and unexpected connection restrictions placed on Ukraine's US-provided Starlink satellite system during drone operations.
brief.why: Trump stated that suspending the sanctions was in the US national interest, driven by soaring domestic fuel costs and inflation ahead of midterm elections. Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev asserted the sanctions would inflict serious damage on global markets, while critics like Congressman Don Beyer accused Trump of betraying Ukraine and surrendering to Vladimir Putin.

brief.what: Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian farmers and an American journalist during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank. A local official reported that 12 Palestinians were injured near the village of Abu Falah, contributing to a season that has seen more than 120 injuries and one Palestinian killed.
brief.who: Masked Israeli settlers carried out the assaults, injuring olive harvesters and Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine, while Israeli forces arrived and dispersed the confrontation.
brief.context: All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law, and unauthorized outposts have increasingly clustered near Palestinian farmland. The United Nations reported that settler attacks over a recent two-week span exceeded the total recorded during the entire previous harvest season.
brief.why: A local landowner stated that settlers target farmers working near village perimeters, amid broader territorial tensions and policies from Israel's pro-settlement government that encourage land claims.
brief.next: The Israeli prime minister's office and military said the incident is under investigation, while the US State Department and The Washington Post have urged thorough inquiries and accountability.

items.title: Evacuation orders as fast-moving California wildfire burns homes
items.summary: Fast-moving wildfires driven by Santa Ana winds and high temperatures have prompted evacuations and damaged or destroyed at least six homes in Southern California. The blazes include the 465-acre Norte Fire and the 2,000-acre Henderson Fire, which forced temporary closures of the I-5 highway.

also.author: The Associated Press
also.title: Coastal homes burn as hot winds fuel California fires
also.note: NPR emphasizes the coastal geography and hot winds driving the destruction of homes.

also.title: Southern California wildfire engulfs homes, prompts evacuation orders
also.note: Al Jazeera focuses on the broader Southern California footprint, homes engulfed, and resultant evacuation directives.

brief.what: Fast-moving wildfires have triggered evacuation orders across Southern California, with the 465-acre Norte Fire damaging or destroying six homes and injuring one firefighter. Additional active blazes include the 147-acre Bryson Fire in Malibu and the Henderson Fire, which exceeded 2,000 acres.
brief.who: Local residents face evacuations, while Division 3 Fire Chief Mark Backoff and firefighting crews battle blazes across multiple counties with support from aerial aircraft.
brief.context: The California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection reported 13 wildfires burning across the state. The Henderson Fire in San Diego County burned land around Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton and forced officials to twice close the I-5 highway.
brief.why: The fires were fanned by fierce Santa Ana winds topping 40mph alongside low humidity, dry vegetation, and unseasonably high temperatures, prompting the National Weather Service to issue red flag warnings and heat advisories.
brief.next: Officials expect dangerous winds to persist into Saturday morning, with temperatures forecast to reach 95F in Southern California.

items.title: Accounts diverge over who ordered limits on Ukraine’s Starshield service
items.author: Clement Charpentreau
items.summary: Ukraine's access to SpaceX's military-grade Starshield satellite service was at least partly restored following speed caps that disrupted drone operations. Disagreement remains over whether the US military or the White House ordered the restrictions, which limited connection speeds to 160 kilometers per hour.

also.author: Ryan Mac
also.title: What Is Starshield, SpaceX’s Military-Grade Satellite Internet Service Ukraine Relies On?
also.note: The New York Times frames the story as an explanatory overview of the Starshield technology and Ukraine's operational reliance on it, rather than focusing on the political dispute over who ordered the speed limits.

brief.what: Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starshield satellite service was at least partly restored after unannounced speed limits of 160 kilometers per hour disrupted drone operations. It remains disputed whether the cap has been completely removed.
brief.who: Key figures include SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, and US President Donald Trump.
brief.context: The 160 km/h cap hindered Ukrainian interceptor drones targeting Russian jet-powered Shahed variants, such as the Geran-4, which fly at 300 to 400 km/h.
brief.why: Musk stated the US government owns and controls Starshield systems, placing operational limits under US military and presidential authority. Reuters reported officials attributing the order to the White House, while an anonymous senior official denied President Trump requested it; Trump had recently criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for raising oil prices.
